summary: This note gives a historical overview of the photoelectric effect and the scientists who helped explain it. It traces Heinrich Hertz's 1887 observation of ultraviolet light producing sparks, Max Planck's 1900 quantization proposal, Albert Einstein's 1905 light-quanta hypothesis, and Robert Millikan's 1914 experimental support. It also notes the Nobel Prizes awarded to Einstein in 1921 and Millikan in 1923.
one_line: Historical account of the photoelectric effect, from Hertz's 1887 observation through Einstein's quantum explanation and the related Nobel Prizes.
key_facts: In 1887, Heinrich Hertz discovered that electrodes illuminated with ultraviolet light create electric sparks more easily.
In 1900, while studying black-body radiation, the German physicist Max Planck suggested that the energy carried by electromagnetic waves could only be released in packets of energy.
In 1905, Albert Einstein published a paper advancing the hypothesis that light energy is carried in discrete quantized packets to explain experimental data from the photoelectric effect.
Einstein's 1905 light-quanta model contributed to the development of quantum mechanics.
In 1914, Robert Millikan's experiment supported Einstein's model of the photoelectric effect.
Albert Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1921 for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.
Robert Millikan was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1923 for his work on the elementary charge of electricity and on the photoelectric effect.
